finding.claim: Broken authorization on PUT /doc/<doc_id>: the handler calls can_edit() but discards its boolean result, so the ownership/editor check is never enforced. Any caller who reaches the handler with a g.user set can overwrite the body of any document. The sibling handler update_title uses require_edit(), which aborts with 403, so this is a missed enforcement rather than a design choice.
finding.source: Any authenticated user (g.user populated by upstream auth middleware, not present in this repo) sends PUT /doc/<doc_id> with a JSON body {"body": "..."} for a document they neither own nor are an editor of. The doc_id is attacker-chosen.
finding.sink: doc["body"] = request.json["body"] at docs.py:20, a write to the shared DOCS store.

trace.note: Route PUT /doc/<doc_id> registered; doc_id is attacker-controlled
doc = DOCS[doc_id] looks up any document with no scoping to the caller
can_edit(g.user, doc) returns a bool that is ignored; no abort(403) on False
Body overwritten unconditionally with attacker-supplied JSON

finding.guards_checked: The correct guard require_edit() (docs.py:11-13) exists and is used in update_title at docs.py:27, but not here. No before_request, decorator, or other auth hook appears in the repo, and no such control is visible on this route. Unauthenticated access would depend on external middleware that is not in the repo. Flask's default behaviour does not enforce anything here. Minor non-security issues were ruled out as exploitable: a missing DOCS key gives a KeyError and a 500 rather than a bypass, and a missing 'body' key gives a 400 or 500.

verdict.guard_found: none (require_edit at docs.py:11-13 aborts 403 but is not called in update_doc; can_edit at docs.py:8 only returns a bool)
verdict.reason: docs.py:19 calls can_edit(g.user, doc) as a bare statement whose bool result is discarded, so docs.py:20 overwrites doc["body"] for any caller who reaches the route, unlike update_title which enforces require_edit at docs.py:27.
